title: Install the mcpindex gate and watch your first HOLD
meta_description: A start-to-finish walkthrough: install the mcpindex gate, see which MCP hosts it wires, then watch it HOLD a silently changed tool contract before your agent acts. Roughly 4 minutes.
h1: Install the gate and watch your first HOLD
outcome: The gate installed and wired into your MCP hosts, and a live contract change held right in front of you, so you know exactly what a HOLD looks like before it matters.

impatient.label: Skip ahead and watch a contract change get held first

body: The tool your agent trusted on Monday can change on Tuesday, with no version bump your client notices. The gate installs locally, pins the declared contract of each tool you wire it in front of on first sight, and HOLDs a call when that contract silently changes, before your agent acts. It is a contract-diff, not a safety verdict, and it holds no credentials. Here is the whole path, start to finish.

steps.heading: Install the gate
steps.body:
Run this in your terminal. It needs uv already installed (`brew install uv`, or see astral.sh). It installs the gate binary and rewrites each MCP host's config so that host's servers launch behind the gate. Free, no account, runs locally.

One limit to know before you run it: the wiring rewrites stdio entries. A server your host reaches over a url is left exactly as it was and shows up as skipped_http in the summary line. Covering those needs the http gateway, which is not wired by this command.

Want to see it before it writes? Run mcpindex-config-wire plan first: it lists every host and entry it would rewrite and changes nothing.

steps.heading: What stays resident, and what does not
steps.body:
The uv command above installs a binary and rewrites config files. Nothing keeps running afterwards.

The one-script install (`curl -fsSL https://mcpindex.ai/install.sh | sh`) does more. It bootstraps uv from astral.sh if uv is missing, and it registers a background watcher as a login item (a launchd agent on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux) that wires any MCP server you add later without asking again. It runs whether or not you accepted the wiring, and there is no flag to skip it.

If you would rather nothing stayed resident, use the uv command. To remove a watcher you already installed: `curl -fsSL https://mcpindex.ai/uninstall.sh | sh`.

steps.heading: Restart your host
steps.body: Quit and reopen the host you use (Claude Desktop, Cursor, and so on) so it reloads the gated config. Nothing changes about how you call your tools. The gate sits in the path and stays quiet until a contract drifts.
steps.troubleshoot: If tools stop appearing after the restart, run `mcpindex-config-wire status` to check the wiring, or `mcpindex-config-wire unwire` to restore every host config. `uninstall.sh` is not written to your machine by either install path; if you used the install script, run `curl -fsSL https://mcpindex.ai/uninstall.sh | sh`, which also removes the watcher unit it registered. Neither path deletes ~/.mcpindex: your pins, your consent answer and your install id stay on disk, and a reinstall reuses the same install id. Remove that directory if you want the id gone too.

steps.heading: Watch a contract change get held
steps.body: Now the part that matters. Pin a tool's contract, apply a change, and watch what the gate does. This is the gate's verdict for five real contract changes, with the posture layer running live in your browser. The verdicts come from the gate's own scenario suite; the diff itself runs on your machine, not here. Try a breaking change and a benign one:

steps.heading: Read the verdict
steps.body: A HOLD means the live contract differs from what you pinned, so the call is paused before your agent acts. A PROCEED means there was no breaking difference (a benign added-optional field can pass through). The verdict is about what changed, never a claim that the tool is safe.

steps.heading: Find the trace on stderr
steps.body: As the gate works it leaves one quiet line per call on your host's stderr, so you can see it is present without it getting in your way.

steps.heading: Your receipts page, and which install path fills it
steps.body: This one-command install wires a proxy, and the proxy does not post receipts today, so by default nothing leaves your host. The wiring command does ask you once whether to join the drift network; answer anything other than y or yes and it stays off. To turn it off later: mcpindex-config-wire wire --repin --drift-telemetry off; setting the variable in your shell will not reach it, because the wiring writes the setting into your MCP host's config entry and that is what the proxy reads. Say yes and each pin and each drift sends a fingerprint of the server and tool, the two contract hashes, the change type, a safety flag, an hour-rounded time, a client tag, and the same random install id your receipts page is keyed to. To turn it off later: mcpindex-config-wire wire --repin --drift-telemetry off; setting the variable in your shell will not reach it. The fingerprint is a key over a public registry, not anonymity. The Python SDK wrapper is the half that posts a credential-blind receipt per gated call, on by default; set MCPINDEX_RECEIPT_INGEST_ENABLED=0 to turn that off. Your receipts page fills up only on the wrapper path. It is credential-blind: the contract hash, the verdict and the action, closed-vocabulary fields about the run and its outcome, and an hour-rounded timestamp, never the arguments, the results, the server name or the URL. Set MCPINDEX_RECEIPT_INGEST_ENABLED=0 to send nothing; the local stderr line keeps working. On the receipt that decision is logged on the trust axis: a PROCEED shows as ALLOW, a HOLD as DENY, an inconclusive as REVIEW. On the wrapper path this page is where you check what the gate did. On this one-command install it stays empty, and the gate's stderr line is where you look instead. Your install id is a random token at ~/.mcpindex/install_id (run: cat ~/.mcpindex/install_id), and your page lives at mcpindex.ai/receipts?id=<install-id>. It fills only on the wrapper path. Treat that URL like a secret: the install id is the only thing gating read access, so anyone holding it can read that install's call log. From gate v0.9.0 the gate also prints a local weekly summary line (calls gated, drift seen, holds) that links the same page; the counters are local-only and nothing about that line is sent anywhere.

deep_link.label: Open your Gate Activity
deep_link.look_for: the tool hash, the verdict (ALLOW, REVIEW, or DENY), and the action, one row per gated call. Paste your install id from ~/.mcpindex/install_id, on this one-command install the page stays empty; it fills only on the SDK wrapper path.

steps.heading: Run it log-only for a week before it blocks anything
steps.body:
The wire command has no posture flag of its own yet. Pass the posture through the proxy command instead, and keep the --from pin the default gives you:

mcpindex-config-wire wire --repin --proxy-cmd "uvx --from mcpindex-gate mcpindex-proxy --posture monitor"

Add ==<version> if you want the pin the default gives you; mcpindex-config-wire status prints the version it wired. Monitor downgrades every drift hold to a note and lets the call through, and the flag survives a later re-wire. Two things still stop a call in monitor: an unreadable pin store, and a bug in the gate's own code. Both fail closed on purpose and neither is settable by posture.

faq.q: Do I need an account to install the mcpindex gate?
faq.a: No. The gate installs locally with one command, needs no account, and holds no credentials. An account only matters later if you opt into cloud tiers or higher limits.

faq.q: What does a HOLD from the gate actually mean?
faq.a: A HOLD means the tool's live declared contract differs from what you pinned on first sight, so the gate pauses the call before your agent acts. It is a contract-diff (this changed), not a claim that the tool is safe or unsafe.

faq.q: Will the gate change how I use my tools?
faq.a: No. It sits in the path and stays quiet, leaving one trace line per call on stderr. You only notice it when a tool's contract changes and it holds the call for you to look at.
